section_summary: This section follows American, British and Dutch responses to Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law and the proposed oil monopoly in Manchuria. Foreign oil companies contest stockholding requirements, seek provisional import plans and coordinate visits by senior representatives. State Department records also document discussions with British officials about joint commercial and diplomatic action.

people.name: Walter C. Teagle
people.role: President of Standard Oil Company of New Jersey

people.name: Stanley K. Hornbeck
people.role: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

people.name: Godber
people.role: British-Dutch oil representative traveling to East Asia

people.name: Orde
people.role: British official consulted about oil policy

subfiles.title: Continuation of report on Japanese and Manchurian petroleum policy
subfiles.about: Japanese officials anticipate foreign retaliation over petroleum restrictions and the Manchurian monopoly.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office reportedly urges slow enforcement of Japan’s petroleum law and doubts that the Manchurian monopoly will be enforced immediately.

subfiles.title: Document file note on Japanese Petroleum Industry Law
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to Parker’s information on the petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Notes that Parker’s cable accords with embassy reporting and cautions about possible price controls.

subfiles.title: Handwritten note on oil representatives’ arrival
subfiles.about: The writer objects to an unannounced appearance by oil representatives in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Calls a surprise arrival a serious mistake; records concurrence.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Walter C. Teagle
subfiles.about: Teagle discusses British intentions and whether to announce the oil representatives’ arrival.
subfiles.summary: Mackay declines to advise company tactics but favors a united American, British and Dutch approach to Japan.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Teagle and Coe
subfiles.about: Oil company and State Department officials discuss coordinated travel and talks in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Participants favor having company representatives meet in Shanghai and travel together to Japan. They await possible British action and discuss uncertainty among Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: Memorandum in regard to Japan
subfiles.about: Company officials consider withholding the required November 15 petroleum returns.
subfiles.summary: London contacts expect British diplomatic pressure and advise foreign firms against submitting returns or opening direct discussions. Standard-Vacuum proposes matching Shell’s stance.

subfiles.title: Harden message from London, November 12
subfiles.about: Shell advises its representatives to defer compliance and avoid premature discussions.
subfiles.summary: Harden relays Shell’s position on Japanese returns, proposed talks and refusal to supply Manchukuo information.

subfiles.title: Harden message from London, November 13
subfiles.about: Harden reports expected British action and urges coordinated company timing.
subfiles.summary: The cable discourages seeking an extension, suggests synchronizing the representatives’ arrival, and supports declining crude-oil quotations for Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Draft cablegram to Yokohama
subfiles.about: Draft advice rejects a November 15 reply and calls for consultation with British interests.
subfiles.summary: Warns that replying could appear to accept provisions threatening the company’s investment.

subfiles.title: File memorandum on Tokyo despatch No. 1042
subfiles.about: The Department reviews the Japanese Foreign Office reply to earlier oil representations.
subfiles.summary: Records that no action is required and that the reply did not satisfy foreign oil interests.

subfiles.title: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: The embassy assesses Japan’s response to foreign objections to its petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Grew finds the response vague on future trade, favorable to domestic refining and silent on stockholding burdens. He reports dissatisfaction among American and British firms, while noting press suggestions that Japan may ease implementation.

subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Office memorandum on the Petroleum Industry Law
subfiles.about: Japan explains operating approvals, allotments, refining permissions, purchases and price regulation.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum promises no arbitrary impairment of existing business while demand grows. It favors refining imported crude in Japan, especially through firms with majority Japanese capital, and reserves powers to purchase stocks or adjust prices.

subfiles.title: Coe letter enclosing Harden’s November 15 cable
subfiles.about: Coe forwards an update on company responses to the Japanese petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Encloses Harden’s cable and thanks Hornbeck for the Department’s assistance.

subfiles.title: Harden message from London, November 15
subfiles.about: Oil representatives agree to seek delay while hearing Japanese officials without commitment.
subfiles.summary: Harden relays a revised plan to request more time for returns, attend an explanatory meeting and meet other senior representatives in Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reply to Coe
subfiles.about: Hornbeck asks about company travel plans and shares a report on Manchukuo oil laws.
subfiles.summary: He requests the decision on a Shanghai meeting and notice to Japanese authorities. He quotes a Mukden report describing licensing, exclusive sales agents and possible government purchase of displaced firms’ equipment.

subfiles.title: Teagle letter on Shell’s delay request
subfiles.about: Teagle reports Shell’s proposal to delay submitting required information.
subfiles.summary: He quotes a cable seeking delay until intergovernmental talks advance and company principals decide.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgement to Teagle
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Teagle’s update on the petroleum-law dispute.
subfiles.summary: Notes receipt of Coe’s related letter and thanks Teagle for continuing updates.

subfiles.title: Phillips conversation with the British Ambassador
subfiles.about: Phillips discusses British-American cooperation on oil problems in Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Phillips says the companies must make their own representations and explains why he expects Britain, with larger combined British-Dutch interests, to take the lead.

subfiles.title: Copy of Phillips conversation with the British Ambassador
subfiles.about: Duplicate record of Phillips’s discussion of British-American oil cooperation.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the memorandum on company initiative and the relative size of British-Dutch interests.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal to Bingham
subfiles.about: Phillips sends Bingham the memorandum of his British Ambassador conversation.
subfiles.summary: Transmits the November 22 memorandum for Bingham’s personal, confidential information.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck telephone conversation with Coe
subfiles.about: Hornbeck asks whether visiting oil representatives will discuss Japan, Manchuria or both.
subfiles.summary: Coe expects discussion of Japan first, lacks definite British plans and reports no new London development beyond a promised Foreign Office move.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck telephone conversation with Wiggin
subfiles.about: Wiggin requests information following a broad British Foreign Office instruction.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck offers to answer more specific questions about the oil situation.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck conversation with Wiggin
subfiles.about: Hornbeck briefs Wiggin on diplomatic exchanges and company consultations.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says the governments have exchanged information on their representations and that Washington awaits British suggestions for cooperation. Wiggin reports seeking clearer instructions from London.

subfiles.title: Copy of Hornbeck conversation with Wiggin
subfiles.about: Duplicate record of the November 19 briefing to Wiggin.
subfiles.summary: Repeats Hornbeck’s account of diplomatic exchanges and his expectation that the British Foreign Office will suggest its preferred next step.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 258 forwarding Goold’s message
subfiles.about: Goold proposes submitting provisional import Form 4 without committing the company.
subfiles.summary: The proposed covering letter reserves a final decision on continuing business in Japan. Goold and British interests believe the compromise may ease the immediate dispute while preserving diplomatic options.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck letter relaying Goold’s message
subfiles.about: Hornbeck forwards Goold’s proposed provisional filing and invites discussion.
subfiles.summary: Unable to reach Coe by telephone, Hornbeck quotes the Tokyo message. He notes a second embassy assessment and suggests sending a representative to Washington.

subfiles.title: Copy of Tokyo telegram No. 258
subfiles.about: Duplicate telegram forwarding Goold’s proposed provisional import filing.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the plan to submit Form 4 conditionally while reserving the company’s decision on future operations.

subfiles.title: Copy of Hornbeck letter to Coe
subfiles.about: Duplicate letter relaying Goold’s message and suggesting a Washington consultation.
subfiles.summary: Quotes the conditional filing proposal and notes that further embassy information could affect decisions by the Department and company.

subfiles.title: Handwritten file note
subfiles.about: A largely illegible note comments on attached petroleum correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The legible fragments do not establish a clear action or conclusion.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 244 on November 15 deadline
subfiles.about: Japanese authorities demand foreign oil firms’ import and storage plans.
subfiles.summary: The firms regard the November 15 deadline and warning about 1935 operations as an ultimatum.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 257 on petroleum-law talks
subfiles.about: The embassy reports Japanese proposals for provisional plans and possible trade guarantees.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials renew the demand for a 1935 import plan but discuss conditional quotas, refining licenses and a possible guarantee of existing trade. Kurusu suggests stronger evidence of the stockholding burden might prompt reconsideration. The embassy asks whether provisional filing would harm diplomatic action.

subfiles.title: Copy of Tokyo telegram No. 257
subfiles.about: Duplicate report of Japan’s provisional-plan proposal and related petroleum-law talks.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the discussion of quotas, refining, stockholding costs and conditional filing; requests the Department’s view.

subfiles.title: Coe letter enclosing company messages
subfiles.about: Coe forwards London and Yokohama messages and discusses whether to link Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Coe leans toward a conditional filing and expects Parker and Walden to focus on Japan’s petroleum law. He seeks Hornbeck’s views before extending their talks to Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Harden message from London, November 23
subfiles.about: Harden reports expected British action and proposes a Shanghai meeting.
subfiles.summary: Says the Foreign Office expects to act soon and suggests Godber, Parker and Walden meet in Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable on Form 4
subfiles.about: Japanese officials propose conditional Form 4 returns while declining to change the law.
subfiles.summary: The office reports renewed warnings, conditional 1935 quotas and no planned compensation for stockholding. Japanese officials suggest that specific evidence of possible foreign withdrawal could prompt reconsideration.

subfiles.title: London telegram No. 603 on concerted oil action
subfiles.about: Dooman reports Orde’s conditions for coordinated British-American oil company action.
subfiles.summary: Orde favors effective private action that requires no formal British government step and treats Japan and Manchuria together. He doubts another immediate official démarche would help.

subfiles.title: Department telegram responding to London report
subfiles.about: The Department updates London on its Manchurian protest and provisional-plan position.
subfiles.summary: It reports a firm aide-mémoire on the Manchurian monopoly, denies any link to naval talks and sees no objection to provisional plans if companies and embassies approve.

subfiles.title: Department telegram instructing further discussion with Orde
subfiles.about: Washington sets out its position on joint action and directs officials to discuss it with Orde.
subfiles.summary: The Department favors close American, British and Dutch consultation and British coordination. It doubts effective export restrictions are presently feasible, asks that company representatives’ talks in Tokyo be prepared diplomatically, and seeks full exchange of plans and views.

subfiles.title: Copy of London telegram No. 603
subfiles.about: Duplicate account of Orde’s views on coordinated oil company action.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the British conditions: effective private measures, no formal government action and treatment of Japan and Manchuria as one problem.
